# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 14 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Wisdom 14

---

**1** Again, one preparing to sail and about to cross savage waves cries out to wood more fragile than the vessel carrying him.

**2** For that vessel was devised by a desire for gain, and wisdom was the craftsman who built it;

**3** but it is your providence, O Father, that steers it, because you have given a path even in the sea, and a safe way through the waves,

**4** demonstrating that you are able to save from every danger, so that even one without experience may put to sea.

**5** Yet it is your will that the works of your wisdom should not be idle; therefore people also entrust their lives to the smallest piece of wood, and passing through the surge on a raft, they come through safely.

**6** For even in the beginning, when arrogant giants were perishing, the hope of the world took refuge on a raft, and guided by your hand left to the age a seed of generations.

**7** For blessed is wood through which righteousness comes.

**8** But the handmade idol is accursed — both it and the one who made it: he, because he made it; it, because though perishable it was named a god.

**9** For equally hateful to God are both the ungodly and his ungodliness,

**10** and both the deed and the one who did it will be punished together.

**11** Therefore upon the idols of the nations too there will be a visitation, because in the creation of God they became an abomination, a stumbling block to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the foolish.

**12** For the devising of idols was the beginning of spiritual fornication, and the invention of them the corruption of life.

**13** For neither did they exist from the beginning, nor will they endure forever.

**14** For through the empty vanity of men they entered the world, and therefore a swift end has been devised for them.

**15** For a father, consumed with grief over a child taken away untimely, made an image of the one so quickly gone, and now honored as a god what was once a dead human being, and handed down to those beneath him secret rites and initiations.

**16** Then in time the ungodly custom was strengthened and observed as law, and carved images were worshipped at the command of rulers.

**17** And when people could not honor them in their presence because they lived at a distance, they imagined the distant appearance and made a visible likeness of the king they honored, so that through their zeal they might flatter the absent one as though present.

**18** But the ambition of the craftsman drove even those who did not know him to intensify their worship,

**19** for he, wishing to please his patron, pressed his art to produce a still finer likeness,

**20** and the crowd, attracted by the beauty of the work, came to regard as an object of worship the one whom shortly before they had honored as a man.

**21** And this became a hidden trap for life, because people enslaved either to misfortune or to tyranny assigned to stones and wood the Name that cannot be shared.

**22** Then it was not enough for them to go astray in knowledge of God; but while living in a great war of ignorance, they call such great evils peace.

**23** For they either perform child-slaughter in their rites, or celebrate hidden mysteries, or hold frenzied revels with outlandish ordinances,

**24** and they no longer guard either the purity of life or the sanctity of marriage; but one destroys another by treachery, or grieves him by adultery.

**25** And over all there reigns a confusion of blood and murder, theft and fraud, corruption, treachery, riot, perjury,

**26** disturbance of good men, ingratitude for kindnesses, pollution of souls, inversion of sex, disorder in marriage, adultery, and debauchery.

**27** For the worship of idols whose names may not be uttered is the beginning and cause and end of every evil.

**28** For they either make merry in exultation, or prophesy lies, or live unrighteously, or readily forswear themselves.

**29** For since they put their trust in lifeless idols, when they swear falsely they expect to suffer no harm.

**30** But just retribution will pursue them on both counts: because they thought wrongly about God in devoting themselves to idols, and because they swore unrighteously in deceit, despising holiness.

**31** For it is not the power of those by whom they swear, but the just penalty of sinners, that always pursues the transgression of the unrighteous.

---

**Council Notes:**

The chapter divides into three movements: the wood of the ship vs. the wood of the idol (vv. 1–8); the origin of idolatry traced to a grieving father (vv. 9–21); and the moral consequences of idolatry enumerated (vv. 22–31).

The etiological account in v. 15 — a father makes an image of his dead child, which becomes a cult object — is one of the most psychologically acute explanations of religion's origin in ancient literature. PNEUMA's rendering ("shattered by grief... the little one so quickly lost") captures this pathos effectively and is partially adopted.

V. 21: "the Name that cannot be shared" (το ακοινωνητον ονομα) refers to the divine Name YHWH — untransferable to idols. LOGOS's "the Name that cannot be shared" and EMET's "the incommunicable Name" both work; "cannot be shared" is preferred as more immediate.

V. 27: "idols whose names may not be uttered" — EMET has "idols that may not be named," LOGOS "unspeakable idols," PNEUMA "nameless idols." The Greek ανωνυμων ειδωλων means literally "nameless/unnameable"; the consensus rendering emphasizes the prohibition rather than absence.

The vice list in vv. 25–26 is kept close to the Greek enumeration without smoothing.
